definition: In computer science, an evolving intelligent system is a fuzzy logic system which improves the own performance by evolving rules.
details: The technique is known from machine learning, in which external patterns are learned by an algorithm. Fuzzy logic based machine learning works with neuro-fuzzy systems. Intelligent systems have to be able to evolve, self-develop, and self-learn continuously in order to reflect a dynamically evolving environment. The concept of Evolving Intelligent Systems (EISs) was conceived around the turn of the century with the phrase EIS itself coined for the first time by Angelov and Kasabov in a 2006 IEEE newsletter and expanded in a 2010 text. EISs develop their structure, functionality and internal knowledge representation through autonomous learning from data streams generated by the possibly unknown environment and from the system self-monitoring. EISs consider a gradual development of the underlying (fuzzy or neuro-fuzzy) system structure and differ from evolutionary and genetic algorithms which consider such phenomena as chromosomes crossover, mutation, selection and reproduction, parents and off-springs. The evolutionary fuzzy and neuro systems are sometimes also called "evolving" which leads to some confusion. This was more typical for the first works on this topic in the late 1990s.

explainer.lead: An evolving intelligent system is a fuzzy or neuro-fuzzy system that continually develops its own rules and internal structure from streaming data and self-monitoring. It is useful when the environment changes and a fixed set of hand-written rules would gradually become outdated.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a weather forecaster who does not just memorize one set of rules, but keeps noticing new weather patterns and updates their notebook. An evolving intelligent system works a bit like that: it watches new information arrive, checks how it is doing, and gradually changes its rules. This helps it keep up when the world around it changes.
tiers.practitioner: An engineer would use a fuzzy or neuro-fuzzy design whose structure and rules can be updated autonomously as data arrives, rather than treating the initial rule base as permanent. Self-monitoring and gradual structural change are central, so evaluation should consider continuing performance in a changing environment. A common pitfall is confusing this with an evolutionary or genetic algorithm based on mutation, crossover, selection, and reproduction.
tiers.paperLevel: In plain-text notation, an EIS at time t can be viewed as EIS_t = (S_t, R_t, K_t), where structure S_t, rules R_t, and internal knowledge K_t are gradually updated from data streams and self-monitoring to improve performance. The phrase EIS was coined by Angelov and Kasabov in a 2006 IEEE newsletter and expanded in a 2010 text. Its defining mechanism is autonomous, gradual development of a fuzzy or neuro-fuzzy system, not the chromosome-based operators of evolutionary and genetic algorithms.

explainer.example: Suppose a fuzzy controller receives sensor readings one after another and initially has only a small rule base. As new patterns appear, it autonomously adds or revises rules and adjusts its internal representation, using self-monitoring to guide further development; later readings are therefore handled by an evolved system rather than the original fixed one.

usedIn.name: Data-stream machine learning
usedIn.detail: Supports continuous learning from data generated by a possibly unknown, changing environment.

usedIn.name: Fuzzy logic systems
usedIn.detail: Provides rule-based systems whose rules can evolve to improve performance.

usedIn.name: Neuro-fuzzy systems
usedIn.detail: Supplies the fuzzy-logic-based machine-learning setting in which EIS structures and knowledge can develop.

explainer.intuition: Instead of designing every rule in advance, let the system gradually build and revise its fuzzy rule base as experience accumulates. Learning concerns not only external patterns but also information gained by monitoring the system itself.
howItWorks: Receive a continuing stream of data from the environment.
Monitor the system's own operation alongside that external data.
Learn autonomously from both sources of information.
Gradually develop the fuzzy or neuro-fuzzy structure, functionality, rules, and internal knowledge representation.
Continue updating so performance can track a dynamically evolving environment.
explainer.whyItMatters: EIS addresses settings where the environment may be unknown and keeps changing, making continuous self-development preferable to a static design. It links performance improvement with changes in the system's structure and knowledge, not just updates to fixed parameters.
misconceptions: EIS is not simply another name for evolutionary or genetic algorithms: it does not depend on chromosomes, crossover, mutation, selection, parents, or offspring.
Calling an evolutionary fuzzy or neuro system 'evolving' can cause confusion, especially in work from the late 1990s.
Learning only fixed external patterns is incomplete as a description: EIS also uses self-monitoring and gradual structural development.
